newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bank Sarasin shifts some assets to stocks.
newsitem.headline: Bank Sarasin shifts some assets to stocks.

text.p: Bank Sarasin & Co has shifted lately some of its managed assets into shares, and out of money market holdings, according to one of its senior managers.
"We have raised the portion invested in shares in (almost) all portfolios," Beat Herger, responsible for quantitative asset allocation at Sarasin, said in an interview.
Bank Sarasin reviews its tactical asset allocation every quarter. In the latest review on December 17, it increased the weighting in favour of shares in most of its various model portfolios.
For example, in the conservative or "defensive" Swiss franc-based portfolio the amount invested in equities was increased to 30 percent from 25 percent.

In the aggressive, or "dynamic" Swiss franc portfolio, the amount was increased to 60 percent from 55 percent, the same strategy employed in the mark-based dynamic portfolio. In its balanced dollar-based portfolio, the amount was raised to 40 percent from 37.5. The weighting remains the same, at 60 percent, in its dynamic dollar-based portfolio.
The shifts in general were done by reducing the amount allocated to money market investments, Herger said.
Herger said at the same time, the bank revised its interest rate outlook, and does not expect any significant increases in interest rates at least until after mid-year.

"We have become more moderate concerning our interest rate and inflation perspectives. Unlike 1996, when some economies improved while others stagnated, we will see in 1997 a global, broad growth at a moderate and restrained pace," he said.
European economies won't see strong growth in 1997, he said. The slow pace of growth coupled with high unemployment was likely to create room for lower interest rates, especially in Germany, he said.
Herger said the current situation in Britain was also favourable for bond investments.
"The Bank of England reacted relatively quickly to higher inflation rates. This should slow growth a bit," Herger said.
Speculation about a British "Euro-entry" may also be positive for sterling bonds and the currency, he said. Currently Britain plans to stay outside the joint European currency.
"The pound is still outside, and officially Britain would like to remain outside," Herger said.
"But there could be some Euro-entry speculation coming up. Even if they (Britain) stay out of the EM, the currency should not come under pressure," Herger said.
"The pound is very interesting, both from a currency and yield perspective," Herger said.
Sterling bonds were preferred in five- to six-year maturities, and U.S. dollar bonds out to three years.
Overall, current strategy favoured European bonds over U.S. bonds, and U.S. bonds over Japanese.
Shares remained attractive despite the chances of a correction, he said. "We cannot rule out a correction on share markets this year, but the environment for shares remains favourable," he said.
With respect to equity asset distribution, Sarasin was emphasising Germany, Holland, the UK and Switzerland, he said. -- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
